extracted.intended_audience: general readers, fans of Stephen King, and aspiring writers seeking insight into his style and methods
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and summarizes Stephen King's stated approaches, stylistic principles, themes, and critical appraisals as presented in his Wikipedia biography — useful for readers or writers studying his craft and influences. Focuses on actionable or evaluative statements about writing, style, and common criticisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stories are 'found things' / excavation metaphor
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories are found things, like fossils in the ground; the writer's job is to use the tools in his or her toolbox to get as much of each one out of the ground intact as possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: King's metaphor: sometimes the fossil is small, sometimes enormous, but the techniques of excavation remain basically the same for short stories and thousand-page novels. Treat story discovery as excavation—preserve what you uncover rather than reshaping it to fit a preconceived plan.

rubrics_metrics.name: Begin with a 'what-if' scenario (premise-driven openings)
rubrics_metrics.description: King often starts with a 'what‑if' scenario, asking what would happen if X (e.g., an alcoholic writer stranded in a haunted hotel; someone could travel in time to alter history).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a provocative situational premise to launch a story; examples on the page include The Shining, The Dead Zone, and 11/22/63. The premise (the situation) drives the narrative and provides the initial imaginative engine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Situation first; characters next (let characters emerge)
rubrics_metrics.description: The situation comes first. The characters—always flat and unfeatured, to begin with—come next. Once these things are fixed in my mind, I begin to narrate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Start by fixing the situation and a rough sense of characters; allow characters to develop and surprise you. King emphasizes not imposing a forced behavior on characters — 'I have never demanded a set of characters that they do things my way. On the contrary, I want them to do things their way.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow outcomes to be unexpected / don't force plot to fit preconceived ends
rubrics_metrics.description: King often has an idea of the outcome, but in most cases the actual outcome is something he never expected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be open to the story leading where it naturally goes rather than forcing characters or plot to satisfy initial plans; this preserves authenticity and can produce surprising, organic resolutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use simile and figurative language to create fresh images
rubrics_metrics.description: The use of simile and other figurative language is one of the chief delights of fiction—by comparing two seemingly unrelated objects we are sometimes able to see an old thing in a new and vivid way.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ original similes and metaphors to produce vivid, memorable imagery (example: King’s image of a clubhouse 'like being inside a Jamaican steel drum'). Figurative language should illuminate and refresh perception rather than distract.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good description: clear seeing to clear writing; fresh images and simple vocabulary
rubrics_metrics.description: He emphasizes the importance of good description, which 'begins with clear seeing and ends with clear writing, the kind of writing that employs fresh images and simple vocabulary.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for descriptive clarity: observe precisely ('clear seeing') and render those observations with straightforward language and striking images. Economy of diction and fresh sensory detail are prioritized over ornate prose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read a lot and write a lot (practice and exposure)
rubrics_metrics.description: If you want to be a writer, you must do two things above all: read a lot and write a lot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: King presents this as foundational: extensive reading to learn models and extensive writing to build craft. This is prescriptive: sustained practice and broad reading underpin improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tell the truth inside the lie (psychological/behavioral authenticity)
rubrics_metrics.description: The story and the people in it may be make believe but I need to ask myself over and over if I've told the truth about the way real people would behave in a similar situation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even in speculative or genre work, strive for believable human behavior and emotional truth; authenticity of reaction and motive matters more than factual realism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ground the extraordinary in ordinary life (theme & resonance)
rubrics_metrics.description: King's characteristic subject is small‑town American life; the intrusion of the extraordinary into ordinary life and how we deal with it. He uses daily life as the frame that makes the picture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anchor horror or speculative elements in everyday details and social reality to heighten emotional impact. Celebrating the ordinary provides contrast and makes the extraordinary more affecting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of authors-as-characters and metafictional devices
rubrics_metrics.description: King often uses authors as characters and has broken the fourth wall (e.g., including himself in The Dark Tower); works like Misery and The Dark Half explore the writer–audience/creative genius relationship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ metafictional or self-referential techniques deliberately to explore themes of authorship, audience, and creativity; these devices can be used as parables about the writing life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy and compact descriptive language (influences: Chandler, Hammett, Ross Macdonald)
rubrics_metrics.description: He gained respect for the power of compact, descriptive language from reading Chandler, Hammett, and Ross Macdonald; he values compact, descriptive language and fresh images.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor concise, potent description over verbosity; learn from classic noir and terse styles to achieve clarity and force in description.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid common faults: bloatedness, illogical plotting, maudlin tone, deus ex machina endings
rubrics_metrics.description: Critics (e.g., S. T. Joshi) have argued King's best-known works can be 'bloated, illogical, maudlin and prone to deus ex machina endings.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be alert to pacing, logical coherence, tonal restraint, and avoid contrived resolutions. The page notes King has tempered some of these faults in later works (since Gerald's Game). Treat these criticisms as cautionary evaluative criteria when assessing or emulating work.
